overview: The Mathematical and Statistical Modeling Education Act aims to update how math is taught in schools by focusing more on mathematical and statistical modeling, which means using math, data and computer tools to solve real-world problems. It directs the National Science Foundation (NSF), the federal agency that funds science research and education, to give competitive awards to colleges and nonprofits to develop and test better ways to teach these skills from preschool through 12th grade, including teacher training, work with real data sets, partnerships with schools and employers, and outreach to rural schools and students underrepresented in science and math. It authorizes $10 million a year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030, paid from money NSF already receives, and the award authority ends September 30, 2029. NSF must also arrange for the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine to study barriers to this kind of teaching, with $1 million a year authorized. As of March 20, 2026, a Senate committee had approved it and it had been sent to a second committee for review.
for: Supporters say employers need workers who can work with data and solve real problems, and research into better ways to teach modeling can help close skills gaps and keep the country competitive.
against: Critics say the federal government should not be steering how local schools teach math, and the money would come out of NSF's existing budget, which could take funding from other research.
